newsitem.title: MEXICO: Galaxy Latin America plans second satellite launch.
newsitem.headline: Galaxy Latin America plans second satellite launch.

text.p: Pay television company Galaxy Latin America said on Monday it plans to launch a second satellite next year that will nearly double the number of channels it can offer subscribers throughout Latin America.

Company officials said the Galaxy VIII-I satellite, worth more than $250 million, will be launched in September, 1997 on a Delta-type rocket. The company successfully launched its Galaxy III-R satellite in December, 1995.
"Galaxy VIII-I will be the second satellite launched in less than two years for DirecTV in Latin America and the Caribbean," Kevin McGrath, chairman of the board for Galaxy Latin America, said.
"After this launch, we will have more capacity than anyone in the medium-term to offer satellite TV coverage in the area," Jose Antonio Rios, CEO of Galaxy Latin America, added.

DirecTV is the brand name for a direct-to-home (DTH) satellite television joint venture between DirecTV International, a subsidiary of Hughes Electronics Corp., and Mexican pay-TV company Multivision, Venezuela's Organizacion Cisneros and Brazil's Televisao Abril.

The new satellite, made by Hughes, will add 32 transponders to the 24 transponders already available with the first satellite. Transponders allow satellites to beam signals to receiving dishes on the ground.

After the second satellite is in place, DirecTV will offer 238 channels -- 145 of digital video, 66 of digital radio and the remainder of open channels that will eventually offer services such as access to the internet and computer games.
DirecTV currently offers 102 channels of digital video and audio to subscribers in Brazil, Venezuela and Mexico.
Company officials said the second satellite would be placed directly above the first in orbit, allowing customers to receive more channels without adjusting their antennas.
Galaxy officials would not say how many subscribers they have signed up so far in the region. Daily Variety newspaper estimates the figure is about 100,000 -- mostly in Brazil.
"We're going to be forced into subscriber disclosure eventually, but we are focusing right now on providing high-quality service...the subscribers will take care of themselves," McGrath told Reuters.

The company expects to begin operations in Costa Rica, Ecuador and Panama later this month, and sees starting up in Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Guatemala and some Caribbean countries during the first few months of next year.
The firm is close to signing a deal for a local partner in Argentina and is also about to finish building a transmission station there, as well, McGrath said.
Galaxy has invested at least $500 million in getting DTH TV up and running in Latin America, McGrath said.
Rios added that the company is close to signing a deal with the U.S. networks allowing selected network programs to be carried on the system.
